14921               	;
14922               	; #if NES
14923               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14924               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14925               	; 	' screen different colours.
14926               	; 	'
14927               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14928               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14929               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14930               	; 	'
14931               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14932               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14933               	; 	'
14934               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14935               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14936               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14937               	; 	'
14938               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14939               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14940               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14941               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14942               	; 	'
14943               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14944               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot
14945               	; 	' overrun vblank the way a single big SCREEN blit can.
14946               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES WHITE ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14947               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14948               	; 	'
14949               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14950               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14951               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14952               	; 	' palette, dark blue and white, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14953               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14954               	; 	'
14955               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14956               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14957               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14958               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.

14960               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14961               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14962               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
14963               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of

14965               	; 	'
14966               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
14967               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
14968               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
14969               	; nes_boxatt:

14971               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85

14973               	; 	NEXT nai
14974               	; 	RETURN

14977               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0
14978               	; 	' $55, NOT $50 -- ALL FOUR QUADRANTS ON P1, not just the bottom two.
14979               	; 	'
14980               	; 	' $50 put the HUD's own row (name row 2) on P1 and left rows 0-1 on P0.
14981               	; 	' That was invisible while text sat on the backdrop, and stopped being so
14982               	; 	' the moment the font gained a PAPER: rows 0-1 are blank cells, and a blank
14983               	; 	' cell is all paper, so they came out in P0's index 1 -- the store's GREEN
14984               	; 	' -- as a green band above the score line. Nothing is drawn up there, so
14985               	; 	' putting the whole byte on P1 costs nothing and the HUD reads as one band
14986               	; 	' of dark blue running into the sky.

14989               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1

15466               	;
15467               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15468               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15469               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15470               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15471               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15472               	; 	'
15473               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15474               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15475               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15476               	; 	'
15477               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15478               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15479               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15480               	; 	'
15481               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15482               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15483               	; 	'
15484               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15485               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15486               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15487               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15488               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15489               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15490               	; 	'
15491               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15492               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15493               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15494               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15495               	; 	'
15496               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15497               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15498               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15499               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

15616               	;
15617               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15618               	; 	'
15619               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15620               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15621               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15622               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15623               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15624               	; 	'
15625               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15626               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15627               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15628               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15629               	; 	' counting stops.
15630               	;
15631               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15632               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15633               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15634               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15635               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15636               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15637               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15638               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15639               	; 	'
15640               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15641               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15642               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15686 F928 F74E     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
15687               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
15688               	; 	'
15689               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
15690               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15691               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15692               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
15693               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
15694               	; 	'
15695               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
15696               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
15697               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
15698               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
15699               	; 	'
15700               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
15701               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15702               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15703               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
15704               	; 	'
15705               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
15706               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
15707               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
15708               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
15709               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
15710               	; 	'
15711               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
15712               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
15713               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it

15987               	;
15988               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15989               	; 	'
15990               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15991               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15992               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15993               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15994               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15995               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15996               	; 	'
15997               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15998               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15999               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
16000               	; 	'
16001               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
16002               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
16003               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
16004               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
16005               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
16006               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
16007               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
16008               	; 	'
16009               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
16010               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
16011               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
16012               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
16013               	; 	'
16014               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
16015               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
16016               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
16017               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
16018               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
16019               	; 	'
16020               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
16021               	; 	' did not finish.
16022               	; pause_beat:
16023               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT

16385               	;
16386               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16387               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16388               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16389               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16390               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16391               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16392               	;
16393               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16394               	; 	'
16395               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16396               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16397               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16398               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16399               	; 	'
16400               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16401               	; 	'
16402               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16403               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16404               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16405               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16406               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16407               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16408               	; 	'
16409               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16410               	; 	'
16411               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16412               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16413               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16414               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16415               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16416               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16417               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16418               	; 	'
16419               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16420               	; 	'
16421               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16422               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16423               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16424               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16425               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16426               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16427               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16428               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16429               	; 	'
16430               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16431               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16432               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16433               	; 	'
16434               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16435               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16436               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16437               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16438               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16439               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16440               	; 	'
16441               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16442               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16443               	; 	'
16444               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16445               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16446               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16447               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16448               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer

16658               	;
16659               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16660               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16661               	; 	'
16662               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16663               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16664               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16665               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16666               	; 	'
16667               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16668               	; 	'
16669               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16670               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16671               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16672               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16673               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16674               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16675               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16676               	; 	'
16677               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16678               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16679               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16680               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16681               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16682               	; 	'
16683               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16684               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16685               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16686               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16687               	; 	#if TI994A
16688               	; 	BANK 2
16689      00F4     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

17163               	; 	' AND THE TITLE'S DISPLAY LIST, for the same reason as the font: walked
17164               	; 	' once by title_draw, at boot and on a return to the title, and never
17165               	; 	' during play. title_draw selects bank 2 around its walk.
17166               	; 	'
17167               	; 	' ITS MESSAGE BOXES DID NOT COME WITH IT. They are the same format and
17168               	; 	' were in the same generated file, which is what made this worth doing
17169               	; 	' carefully: they are walked when a ROUND ENDS, mid-game, so on bank 2
17170               	; 	' they would have returned bytes from the wrong page at the moment a life
17171               	; 	' is lost -- and with no error at build or run time. gentitle.py now
17172               	; 	' writes them to title.bas below, which stays in bank 1.
17173               	; 	INCLUDE "titledl.bas"
17174               	; 	' ==================================================
17175               	; 	' THE TITLE SCREEN, AS A DISPLAY LIST
17176               	; 	' Generated by assets/gentitle.py -- do not edit here.
17177               	; 	'
17178               	; 	' row, col, length, then `length` bytes; 255 ends.
17179               	; 	' Walked by title_draw only.
17180               	; 	'
17181               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2, with the fonts, because it is read ONCE
17182               	; 	' -- at boot and on a return to the title. title_draw
17183               	; 	' selects bank 2 around its walk and restores bank 1.
17184               	; 	' The message boxes in title.bas are the same format and
17185               	; 	' CANNOT come with it: they are read when a round ends.
17186               	; 	' ==================================================
17187               	;

17419               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
17420               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17421               	; 	'
17422               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17423               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17424               	; 	' being small sprites.
17425               	; 	'
17426               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
17427               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
17428               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17429               	; 	'
17430               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
17431               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17432               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
17433               	;
17434               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68

18694               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
18695               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
18696               	; 	'
18697               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
18698               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
18699               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
18700               	; 	'
18701               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
18702               	; 	' blit is
18703               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
18704               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
18705               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
18706               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
18707               	; 	'
18708               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
18709               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
18710               	; 	'
18711               	; 	' template ids:
18712               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
18713               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
18714               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
18715               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
18716               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
18717               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
18718               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
18719               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
18720               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
18721               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
18722               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
18723               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
18724               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
18725               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
18726               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
18727               	;
18728               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes

19345               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19346               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19347               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19348               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19349               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19350               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19351               	; #if NES
19352               	; nes_sky2c:
19353               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9

19356               	; #endif

19359               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19360               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19361               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19362               	; 	'
19363               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19364               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19365               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19366               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
